newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria sees inflation cut to seven percent in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Algeria sees inflation cut to seven percent in 1997.

text.p: The Algerian government foresees inflation being brought down to seven percent in 1997 from 16.5 percent at the end of 1996, according to a government note on the annual review of its programme.
The official news agency APS on Tuesday reported that the government also said the programme to liberalise prices on basic consumer items had almost been completed.
Since 1995, when annual inflation hit 29 percent, the government has been striving to shift the economy to a free market under a three-year accord with the International Monetary Fund.
Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia said at the weekend that 1997 inflation would not top 10 percent.

APS said the government's review showed foreign currency reserves reached $4.23 billion in the first 11 months of the year -- enough to cover four months of imports. Ouyahia had said foreign reserves at the end of 1996 stood at $4 billion.

The foreign currency reserves level for 1996 was a record high and double 1995. The previous high was in 1981 when Algeria piled up about $3.5 billion, thanks to exceptional crude oil prices because of the Gulf War between Iran and Iraq.
